ownership.central_bank: Federal Reserve Banks (12 regional Reserve Banks)
ownership.owners: Commercial banks that are members of the Federal Reserve System hold stock in their District's Reserve Bank; holding a set amount of stock is by law a condition of membership. The Board's FAQ states the System 'is not owned by anyone'. The stock may not be sold or pledged as collateral and does not carry the control and financial interest of common stock; member banks elect six of the nine directors on each Reserve Bank board.
ownership.dividend_or_profit_note: Federal Reserve Act section 7 (12 U.S.C. 289): stockholders with total consolidated assets over $10 billion (inflation-adjusted) receive the smaller of 6% or the high yield of the 10-year Treasury note at the last auction; stockholders at or below that receive 6%; dividends are cumulative. Aggregate surplus is capped at $6,785,000,000 and earnings beyond that go to the Treasury general fund.
ownership.source_title: Federal Reserve Board FAQ 'Who owns the Federal Reserve?'; Federal Reserve Act section 7; St. Louis Fed 'Who Owns the Federal Reserve Banks?'

ownership.owners: Share capital CHF 25 million in 100,000 registered shares of CHF 250. End-2024: cantons and cantonal banks held just under 51% (50.9%); private sector 27.0% (26,739 shares); shares pending registration of transfer 22.0%. 26 cantons and 24 cantonal banks held 75.4% of voting shares. The Confederation is not a shareholder. Voting rights of shareholders outside the public sector are capped at 100 shares.
ownership.dividend_or_profit_note: Dividend may not exceed 6% of share capital (CHF 15 per share, the legal maximum, proposed for 2024 and again for 2026). Of the remaining profit distribution, one-third goes to the Confederation and two-thirds to the cantons (CHF 3 billion distributed for 2024).
ownership.source_title: SNB Annual Report 2024, Business report section 1.2; SNB 'The SNB as a joint-stock company'

ownership.owners: Capital of 100 million yen; the government holds 55% (at least 55 million yen under the Bank of Japan Act) and private investors hold 45%. Subscription certificates trade as a listed issue on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. Holders have no role in managing the Bank; on liquidation they may claim only paid-up capital plus any special reserve.
ownership.dividend_or_profit_note: Dividend rate requires Minister of Finance approval and may not exceed 5% per year of paid-up capital (Act Article 53(4)).
ownership.source_title: Bank of Japan, Outline of the Bank; BOJ 'oshiete' FAQ a12

ownership.owners: Share capital EUR 10 million in 400,000 shares. 200,000 registered, non-transferable shares are held by the Belgian State (by law since 1948). The other 200,000 shares trade freely on Euronext Brussels (ISIN BE0003008019, ticker BNB). The Bank knows of no other holding of 5% or more of voting rights.
ownership.dividend_or_profit_note: First dividend of 6% of capital plus a second dividend set by the Council of Regency at 50% of net proceeds from the portfolio held against reserves (policy of 22 July 2009, adapted 23 March 2016). Most recent net dividend shown: EUR 1.05 per share paid 27 May 2024.

ownership.owners: Capital EUR 7.5 billion in registered quotas of EUR 25,000 (300,000 quotas per the participant list). Eligible holders: banks and insurers with registered and head office in Italy, banking foundations (d.lgs. 153/1999), Italian social security bodies, and pension funds (d.lgs. 252/2005). Holding cap 5% since 1 January 2022 (3% under Law 5/2014); quotas above the cap carry no voting or economic rights. List at 30 April 2026 has 173 holders; largest: UniCredit 15,000 quotas; INARCASSA, Fondazione ENPAM and Cassa Forense 14,800 each; Intesa Sanpaolo 14,736; CNPADC 11,000; BPER 9,765; ICCREA 9,367; Generali Italia 9,084; INPS, INAIL, Cassa di Sovvenzioni e Risparmio del personale della Banca d'Italia and Cassa di Risparmio di Asti 9,000 each.
ownership.dividend_or_profit_note: Up to 6% of capital may be paid to participants; dividends on quotas above the cap go to statutory reserves.
ownership.source_title: Banca d'Italia 'Partecipanti al Capitale' and 'Partecipanti al capitale della Banca d'Italia al 30 aprile 2026' (PDF)

ownership.exchange: Over-the-counter share trading facility (delisted from JSE 2 May 2002; OTC facility live since 1 October 2005)
ownership.owners: 2,000,000 issued shares held by just over 800 shareholders. No shareholder, alone or with associates, may hold more than 10,000 shares. Only South African residents may vote, at one vote per 200 shares. Shareholders have no role in monetary policy, financial stability policy, or regulation. The SARB page does not state any government shareholding. Nationalisation: an EFF private member's South African Reserve Bank Amendment Bill to have the state buy out private shareholders was before the Standing Committee on Finance (meeting 6 September 2023; public hearings 2 July 2025, where National Treasury called it 'a forced takeover'). No vote or enactment was found in sources opened.
ownership.dividend_or_profit_note: Annual dividend of not more than 10 cents per share; surplus earnings after provisions, tax, reserve transfers and dividends are paid to the South African government.
ownership.source_title: SARB 'Shareholder Information'; PMG Standing Committee on Finance meeting 6 Sep 2023; Daily Maverick 2 Jul 2025

ownership.owners: 19,864,886 shares (264,865 voting rights; 75 shares per vote). The Greek State owns 1,774,088 shares (8.93%) after taking over DEKA S.A.'s 1,309,210 shares under Law 3943/2011. Since financial year 2013, financial rights including dividends are suspended for entities supervised by the Bank, their affiliates, directors and close relatives.
ownership.dividend_or_profit_note: 93rd AGM (6 April 2026): 2025 net profit EUR 257,741,433; dividend EUR 0.6720 per share (EUR 13,349,203); EUR 244,392,230 transferred to the Government.
ownership.source_title: Athens Exchange announcements: Greek State holding after DEKA dissolution; Decisions of the 93rd Annual Ordinary General Meeting of Shareholders of the Bank of Greece
ownership.as_of: 2026-04-06 (state share figure from undated post-2011 announcement)

ownership.central_bank: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
ownership.owners: Capital TRY 25,000 in 250,000 shares. End-2025: Class A (Turkish Treasury only; by law not below 51%) 55.12%; Class B (national banks operating in Türkiye) 23.25%; Class C (non-national banks and privileged companies; max 15,000 shares) 2.51%; Class D (Turkish commercial enterprises and Turkish real and legal persons) 19.12%. No privileged companies are shareholders.
ownership.source_title: CBRT Annual Report 2025, Part 1 General Information

ownership.central_bank: Central Bank of the Republic of San Marino
ownership.owners: The BCSM describes itself as a body of private legal nature with mixed public and private participation. The State is the principal shareholder; San Marino banks, financial and insurance companies may hold a minority stake. No percentages were found on the BCSM site.

arrangements.name: West African CFA franc (WAEMU/UMOA) – France cooperation
arrangements.issuer: BCEAO (Dakar); convertibility guaranteed by the French Treasury
facts: The currency (XOF) is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs.
France gives an unconditional and unlimited convertibility guarantee through advances to the central bank if its foreign exchange reserves run out.
A new cooperation agreement was signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019, replacing the 1973 agreement; France stated the reform would enter into force in 2020.
The 2019 agreement ended the centralisation of BCEAO reserves at the French Treasury, ending the requirement that the BCEAO hold at least 50% of its reserves there.
The BCEAO's operations account at the French Treasury was closed in April 2021 (French Senate report); the Treasury page states it has had no operations account since January 2020.
France approved the agreement by Law no. 2021-108 of 3 February 2021.

France withdrew its representatives from the BCEAO board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the UMOA Banking Commission; one independent member of the Monetary Policy Committee is appointed in consultation with the French government.
The agreement provides that the currency will be renamed 'ECO'; the Banque de France page says the name 'is set to change' at member states' will, i.e. the CFA franc name remains in use.
ECOWAS Convergence Council (7 September 2026) kept 2027 as the target launch year for an ECOWAS single currency named the ECO.

arrangements.name: Central African CFA franc (CEMAC/UMAC) – France cooperation
arrangements.issuer: BEAC (Yaoundé); convertibility guaranteed by the French Treasury
facts: The currency (XAF) is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs; the euro replaced the French franc as anchor on 1 January 1999 with no change in parity.
France provides an unlimited convertibility guarantee, committing euro funds if the sub-region cannot pay for imports in foreign currency.
The BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves in its operations account at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007).

Mandatory deposits earn the ECB marginal lending facility rate (stated as 0.25% since 16 March 2016); amounts above earn the ECB main refinancing rate; holdings are protected against euro depreciation against the SDR.
France designates two BEAC administrators and two Monetary Policy Committee members, the same number as each of the six CEMAC states.

A France–CEMAC ministers and governors meeting on 17 March 2026 discussed reserves, public finances and integration; the French Treasury's account records no decision changing the operations account, reserve deposit, French representation or currency name. The next meeting in this format is planned for 2027.
The CFA franc was devalued 50% on 11 January 1994.

arrangements.name: Comorian franc – France cooperation
arrangements.issuer: Banque Centrale des Comores; convertibility guaranteed by the French Treasury
facts: The France–Comoros monetary cooperation agreement was signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979; it bases cooperation on an unlimited guarantee by France of the currency issued by the BCC.
The 1979 agreement set the parity at 1 Comorian franc = 0.02 French francs; the current rate is EUR 1 = 491.968 KMF.
The BCC must deposit 65% of its foreign exchange reserves with the French Treasury.

Under statutes in force since March 2025, France designates two of six Board members, two of four Banking Supervision Committee members and two of four Monetary Policy and Reserve Management Committee members.
The Comorian franc was devalued 33% on 11 January 1994.

arrangements.name: Cabo Verde escudo – Portugal exchange rate cooperation agreement
arrangements.issuer: Banco de Cabo Verde; credit facility from the Portuguese Treasury
facts: The Acordo de Cooperação Cambial was signed on 13 March 1998.
The peg was 0.55 CVE per Portuguese escudo and became CVE 110.265 per euro.

The Portuguese Treasury provides a short-term credit facility of EUR 27.5 million, expandable to EUR 45 million, with drawdowns capped at EUR 5 million; Cabo Verde must transfer reserves equal to 35% of the amount requested.
Banco de Portugal states the facility creates no obligation for Banco de Portugal or any Eurosystem institution to intervene.

sources.title: Banco de Portugal, Revista de Estudos Económicos (April 2020) – Acordo de Cooperação Cambial entre Portugal e Cabo Verde

arrangements.name: Euro area / Eurosystem
facts: Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, making 21 EU Member States that use the euro.
The Bulgarian National Bank joined the Eurosystem and its governor took a seat on the ECB Governing Council.
The Bulgarian lev conversion rate is 1.95583 lev per euro.

sources.title: ECB press release, 1 January 2026

arrangements.name: Euro use by non-EU states under monetary agreements with the EU
facts: Monaco may issue euro coins up to 1/500th of the quantity minted in France each year.
San Marino may issue euro coins up to a maximum annual face value of EUR 1,944,000.
Vatican City may issue euro coins up to a maximum annual face value of EUR 1 million.
Andorra may issue its own euro coins from July 2013 under its monetary agreement with the EU.
The IMF AREAER 2023 classification lists Andorra and San Marino as having no separate legal tender with the euro as anchor.

sources.title: EUR-Lex summary – Exchange rate matters and monetary agreements with the euro area
Deutsche Bundesbank Exchange rate statistics, table VI (from IMF AREAER 2023, Table 4)

arrangements.name: Unilateral euroisation – Montenegro
facts: The Deutsche Mark became parallel legal tender on 2 November 1999 and sole legal tender on 1 January 2001.
The euro became the official means of payment in March 2002 through full conversion.
The Central Bank of Montenegro describes this as unilateral euroisation entered before ECOFIN adopted a position against unilateral euroisation.

The CBCG does not issue euros, is not an ESCB member and cannot access Eurosystem emergency liquidity assistance; it has a Eurosystem repo line (EUREP) of up to EUR 250 million and a EUR 100 million BIS repo line.

sources.title: Central Bank of Montenegro – Euroisation

arrangements.name: Unilateral euroisation – Kosovo
facts: An UNMIK regulation of September 1999 approved use of the Deutsche Mark; the Central Bank of Kosovo states the mark was unilaterally adopted with no negotiation with the Bundesbank or ECB.
Kosovo replaced the Deutsche Mark with the euro in 2002, with the changeover completed on 28 February 2002 in cooperation with the ECB and some euro area central banks.

sources.title: Central Bank of the Republic of Kosovo – Kosovo's experience in euroisation of its economy

arrangements.name: Official dollarization (US dollar as sole legal tender)
facts: The IMF AREAER 2023 classification (end-April 2023) lists Ecuador, El Salvador, Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Palau, Panama and Timor-Leste as having no separate legal tender with the US dollar as anchor.

Ecuador adopted the US dollar in January 2000 at 25,000 sucres per dollar under the Ley para la Transformación Económica (Registro Oficial Suplemento 34, 13 March 2000); Article 94 of the Código Orgánico Monetario y Financiero (2014) makes the dollar the currency of transactions.
In El Salvador, legal reforms made private-sector acceptance of Bitcoin voluntary and tax payments payable only in US dollars, listed as prior actions for the IMF EFF approved on 26 February 2025.

arrangements.name: Liechtenstein – Swiss franc currency treaty
facts: The 1980 Currency Treaty with Switzerland declares the Swiss franc the official tender of Liechtenstein.
The Swiss National Bank serves as Liechtenstein's national bank; certain Liechtenstein banks and investment undertakings report to the SNB for monetary policy purposes.

sources.title: Liechtenstein Financial Market Authority – Bilateral cooperation: Switzerland

arrangements.name: Zimbabwe – multicurrency system
arrangements.issuer: Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (ZiG) alongside foreign currencies
facts: Zimbabwe operates a multicurrency system in which foreign currency circulates alongside the ZiG.

In February 2026 the RBZ dropped its fixed 2030 date for ending the multicurrency system in favour of conditions (inflation, 3–5 months of import cover, ZiG stability); the governor said US dollar contracts will continue to be paid in USD.
The RBZ 2026 Mid-Term Monetary Policy Statement put progress on eight conditions for a mono-currency at a weighted 50.1% and said this does not signal an immediate transition.

sources.title: Nehanda Radio, 27 Feb 2026
The Herald, 23 Aug 2026

arrangements.name: Hong Kong Linked Exchange Rate System
arrangements.issuer: Hong Kong Monetary Authority (US dollar anchor)
facts: The Linked Exchange Rate System began on 17 October 1983 at HK$7.80 per US$1.
Since May 2005 the HKMA sells HK dollars at 7.75 (strong-side convertibility undertaking) and buys at 7.85 (weak side).
The Monetary Base is fully backed by US dollar assets in the Exchange Fund.

arrangements.name: Brunei–Singapore Currency Interchangeability Agreement
arrangements.issuer: Monetary Authority of Singapore / Brunei Darussalam Central Bank
facts: The agreement was established in 1967.
BDCB and MAS accept each other's notes and coins from banks and exchange them at par and without charge into their own currency; banks in both countries accept the other currency for deposit at par.
The IMF AREAER 2023 classification lists Brunei Darussalam as a currency board.

arrangements.name: Djibouti franc currency board
arrangements.issuer: Banque Centrale de Djibouti (US dollar anchor)
facts: The Djibouti franc was created in March 1949 outside the franc zone.
The peg is US$1 = 177.721 Djibouti francs.
The currency is backed 100% by US dollars.

sources.title: Banque Centrale de Djibouti – presentation 'Influence mutuelle'

arrangements.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina convertible mark currency board
arrangements.issuer: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina (euro anchor)
facts: The CBBH is organised on the currency board model; KM is issued only against purchase with convertible foreign currency.
The official rate is EUR 1 = KM 1.95583.
Monetary liabilities may never exceed the CBBH's foreign currency assets.

sources.title: CBBH – 20 years of KM peg to the euro

arrangements.name: Eastern Caribbean Currency Union
arrangements.issuer: Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (US dollar anchor)
facts: The ECCB is the monetary authority for Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
The ECCB agreement was signed on 5 July 1983 and the Bank was commissioned on 1 October 1983.
The EC dollar has been fixed at EC$2.70 = US$1.00 since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling to the US dollar.
Section 24(2) of the ECCB Agreement Act requires an external reserve of not less than 60% of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities.
The IMF AREAER 2023 classification lists the ECCU members as a currency board.

arrangements.name: Common Monetary Area
facts: The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

sources.title: BIS Papers No 17 – L. van Zyl, South Africa's experience of regional currency areas and the use of foreign currencies
